column1: # One line per version of HYPERCOLOR ASTEROIDS, saying what happened to the
# game. Appended by tools/tagline.sh when a version lands, read by
# tools/chronicle.sh into the book, and never rewritten: once a line is in
# here it is the record, even after the script that first wrote it changes its
# Which is the invitation. If the machine gave your version a limp line, edit
# it here and it stays edited. If you would rather not leave it to chance, put
# a  Tagline: <line>  in the commit message and that is what lands.

column2: <what happened to the game>
The cabinet arrives in one file, and it already knows how to kill you.
The game asks who is flying now, and it remembers what they did.
The cabinet keeps score with slightly different arithmetic now.
The seat cards have faces on them, and picking somebody else's feels like a decision.
The panels went to glass, and the field drifts past behind everything you read.
The rules of the field changed while nobody was flying.
Your name is on a card before you have flown, under the words no traps laid.
Ten bands share the cabinet and you do not get to choose which one turns up.
The splash screen grew a second column and a floor. PRESS ENTER stopped moving.
A rule was taken out, looked at, and put back differently.
Every card and row on the splash answers with a note, in whatever key tonight is in.
David Friedrich taught the ambushes to sign their work.
The sign in the corner stopped lying about the room behind it.
The field guide says the same things in half the words.
The splash screen stopped describing the ship and showed it.
ESC is a door now: it stops the field, shows you the run, and costs you the record if you walk.
The cabinet put its name up. A rock three colours out of true is holding it.
The ledger learned mercy - three clean landings ease a bend, and the record still says what happened.
The cabinet keeps score with slightly different arithmetic now.
A tape remembers whose seat it was sealed in, and no one pilot's ambushes own the evening.
The rules of the field changed while nobody was flying.
The field guide went back to listing the field, and stopped explaining the furniture.
The bookkeeping of the cabinet moved a foot to the left.
The tape names every ambush that fired and who laid it, so mischief is a scored game now.
The rules of the field changed while nobody was flying.
Nobody's ambushes fire at you until you have laid one of your own.
The bookkeeping of the cabinet moved a foot to the left.
Versions landed, ambushes laid and flights taped turn up as trim on your hull.
A rule was taken out, looked at, and put back differently.
The bomb comes every other wave now, and the big rocks only crack.
The rules of the field changed while nobody was flying.
David taught the splash screen the difference between a warning and a trophy.
The cabinet keeps score with slightly different arithmetic now.
The splash is one screen you scroll, and the cabinet finally explains itself to strangers.
Somebody rewrote a rule the game had been taking for granted.
The panel counts the rules for you, and the board has been keeping the register all along.
The bookkeeping of the cabinet moved a foot to the left.
A link to the cabinet arrives somewhere else with the lights on.
The bookkeeping of the cabinet moved a foot to the left.
The splash screen learned the difference between reading and pressing.
Somebody rewrote a rule the game had been taking for granted.
Fifteen rules on the panel, and the newest one only asks when somebody else last flew.
The field goes after whoever is top of the board, and the only way down is somebody else's better evening.
A trap can carry somebody's name without being aimed at them, and one carries Malte's.
You can call somebody out, and nothing happens at all until they sign it back.
The board says whether nobody has flown or nobody has built the book, which are different evenings.
The scoreboard climbed down off the wall and into the field.
Something opens a little way off, counts to four, and pulls the neighbourhood into it.
The field stood up. A rock has a far side now, and near the edge you can see round it.
The kraken swims under the rocks, a mine is a hole in the floor, and the salvage still will not light up.
A tape seals the field it was flown under, bends and mercy included.
A key that did nothing now does something. The colours moved as well.
Flying alone, you get a mouse and a reticle that drags a comet behind it.
A trap was set by somebody who will never meet it. An ambush came along with it.
Every trap in the building is an event now, and nothing else changed.
The field guide has shelves, and no row on it runs off the bottom of a laptop.
Everybody the cabinet has heard of gets a card, and the panel is one height at thirty pilots or three.
The band stops coming apart in the fourth minute, and comes back when you return to the tab.
The splash stopped stuttering under a thumb, and stopped fading out the panel you were reading.
The room on the splash was bigger than it was letting on, and the book had been leading with a picture from six versions ago.
Six buttons on a phone, and for the first time one of them shoots.
Clear a wave and the ship spends the pause travelling, and the next one arrives out of the depth.
